title: Permissions, owners, groups, sudo and umask

videos.script: Permission denied. You have seen it four times already in this course, and until now the honest answer was that lesson four would explain it. This is lesson four. {{denied}} Here is the whole system, stated once before we take it apart. Every file on Linux has an owner and a group. Every file carries nine bits, in three sets of three: what the owner may do, what the group may do, what everybody else may do. Read, write, execute. That is it. That is the entire model, and it has protected every Unix machine for fifty years on twelve bits and a couple of extras. {{model}} Two things make it harder than it sounds, and they are the two this lesson spends its time on. The first is that only one of the three sets applies to you — the first one that matches — and it is not the most generous one. You will meet a file whose group can write it, whose owner cannot, and be genuinely surprised. {{one-set}} The second is that the bits mean something different on a directory. Execute on a file means run it. Execute on a directory means something else entirely, and until that clicks, half of what you meet will look arbitrary. {{directories}} We will read a mode character by character, do the arithmetic that turns it into 755, and then meet root — and `sudo`, which is how you become root for exactly one command instead of for an evening. {{sudo}} By the end, a denial should stop being a wall and start being a sentence you can finish out loud. {{title}}

Five refusals, and they have five different causes. The words on the screen are nearly identical every time, and what I want you to take from this is how you tell them apart. {{open}} One. A script that will not run. Permission denied, and the listing shows rw minus r minus minus r minus minus. No x anywhere. Nothing is allowed to execute this, including me, and chmod plus x is the whole fix. {{one}} Two. A file I own, that my own group can write, that I cannot write. Look at the mode — r minus minus, then rwx, then rwx. I am the owner, so the owner's three characters apply, and the fact that I am also in that group buys me nothing. The first match wins, and it is not the most generous one. {{two}} Three. A file anybody may read, that nobody but me can reach. The file is six four four. The directory above it is seven hundred. Read permission on a file you cannot get to is a promise nobody can collect on, and this is the one people spend an hour on. {{three}} Four. A directory I can list but not enter, and beside it one I can enter but not list. Read without execute gives you the names and nothing else. Execute without read gives you the contents, if you already know what they are called. Two bits, two completely different half-permissions. {{four}} Five, and this is the one that catches everybody exactly once. Sudo echo x, redirect into slash root. Permission denied — and look at who is speaking. Bash. Not echo, not sudo. The redirect belongs to the shell, and the shell is still me. Sudo sh minus c, with the whole thing quoted, and it works. {{five}} Five denials. Same two words, five different questions. The habit is to read the rest of the line before you reach for sudo.

Twelve bits, and you can read them now. {{open}} The thing to carry is the question rather than the table. When something is refused, ask three things in this order. Who am I — id, and look at the groups, not just the name. Which of the three sets applies to me — owner, group, or everybody else, and only one of them does. And is it the file that is refusing, or the directory I had to walk through to reach it. That third question is the one nobody asks, and it is the answer about half the time. {{three-questions}} Two habits are worth building tonight. The first: when you are about to chmod something to seven seven seven, stop. Seven seven seven is almost never the answer — it is the shape of somebody who could not work out which bit was missing, and it leaves a file the whole machine can rewrite. Work out the bit. {{777}} The second: sudo is for one command. Not for a session, not for an evening. Every minute you spend as root is a minute where a typo is permanent, and the discipline of typing five characters each time is what keeps that minute short. {{sudo}} And the honest note about where this model runs out. Twelve bits cannot say person A and person B but nobody else. That is what ACLs are for, and you now know the plus sign in a listing that tells you one is there. SELinux and AppArmor sit above all of this and will refuse things the bits allow — if a denial makes no sense and the bits look right, that is where to look next. {{limits}} Next lesson is users and services: where accounts actually live, and how a thing that runs without anybody logged in gets started, stopped and watched. {{next}} Before that, the drill. Fifteen of them, and most are a mode and a user, and the question is what happens.
